newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss industrialist denounces Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss industrialist denounces Holocaust fund.

text.p: A leading Swiss industrialist and right-wing politician injected more controversy into the debate about a Holocaust fund by declaring on Friday the Swiss should not apologise for their business dealings in World War Two.
Christoph Blocher, chairman of the Swiss chemicals company EMS Chemie and a member of parliament, said that contributing to a fund for Holocaust survivors was an admission of guilt.

Switzerland had no reason to apologise for doing business with Nazi Germany in order to survive as a neutral country during the war, Blocher said in answer to reporters' questions at a news conference on his company's 1996 results.
"The trade policy was not false, it was legal, correct and necessary for Switzerland's survival...I want to send the clear message that reparation or an apology is out of the question," Blocher said.
The debate began almost immediately after the nation's three biggest banks announced earlier this month they were donating 100 million Swiss francs ($68 million) to start up the fund.
At the same time they also encouraged both the government and the private sector to contribute.

The decision to set up the fund was aimed at defusing controversy while helping to repair the Swiss banking industry's image, bruised by accusations of hoarding money in accounts left by Holocaust victims.

The banks deny they deliberately kept the money from Holocaust victims' heirs, but reached an agreement with the World Jewish Congress last May to authorise a probe by an independent panel with unprecedented powers to lift bank secrecy in order to search historical records.

The federal government has delayed a decision on joining in while it seeks broad political support for the step, but the cabinet agreed on Wednesday to administer the fund together with the World Jewish Restitution Organisation.

Other banks and private industry in Switzerland have in recent weeks lined up to pledge their support for the fund, which they hope will help restore the good name of Switzerland and its business community.
But Blocher argued that the Swiss should question the idea of using taxpayers' money to make donations to such a fund.
"Why are we paying? The people will want to know why they would have to pay," Blocher said of the discussion on government contribution to the fund.
"The point is not about Switzerland's trade policy, the point is whether Switzerland stole money that didn't belong to it," Marvin Hier, dean of the Simon Wiesenthal Centre, said from Los Angeles.

"Switzerland knew going into the war that the Nazis had between $70 million to $100 million in reserves in gold and in 1943 and 1944 the Nazis shipped to Swiss banks more than $400 million in gold," Hier added.
But the Blick, Switzerland's largest daily, also suggested that the Swiss public is fed up with the issue.
The bold headline: "D'Amato, That's Enough" was splashed across the front page of the newspaper's Friday edition.
The headline and accompanying article came in response to the most recent comments by U.S Senator Alfonse D'Amato, the most vociferous critic of Swiss banks over their role during World War Two.

"The world has already rendered its verdict, the Swiss were guilty. We're now debating the penalty and the penalty should fit the crime," D'Amato said on Wednesday about the government's decision to manage the fund.

The Swiss government will decide whether to join the fund when it has the results in the next few months of an independent study of central bank gold purchases from Nazi Germany and Berne's wartime policy of turning back Jewish refugees from the Holocaust.
